title: Simca P60 Étoile, Élysée, Montlhéry and Monaco: the useful differences
author: Caramagnols
excerpt: Economy Étoile, family Élysée, sporting Montlhéry or two-door Monaco: body style, engine, trim and model year separate the principal versions of the P60.
content:
Étoile, Élysée, Montlhéry and Monaco are not four interchangeable decoration packs. Each name combines a body style, an engine and a place in the range. Annual changes create the difficulty: a 1959 Montlhéry does not have exactly the same mechanical specification as a 1962 Montlhéry Spéciale, while owners continued to call the later Aronde Rush body a P60.

The first question is the number of doors. Étoile, Élysée and Montlhéry are four-door saloons. Monaco is a two-door coach with a lower-looking profile and the richest closed-body presentation. That basic distinction eliminates many fanciful classified descriptions. Engine and trim can then narrow the identity.

Four names and four positions

VersionBodyPurposePriority check
Étoile 6Four-door saloonEconomy model, 1,090 cc and 6 French fiscal horsepowerSimpler trim and thin mouldings on early P60s
ÉlyséeFour-door saloon7 CV family model at the centre of the range1,290 cc engine and model-year equipment
MontlhéryFour-door saloonSporting version with a more highly tuned engineEngine type, carburettor and version-specific components
MonacoTwo-door coachUpper trim and sporting imageBody, broad mouldings and upholstery

The table describes the main families, not every derivative. Depending on the year, Simca also offered Étoile 7, Étoile 6 Super, Montlhéry Spéciale and Monaco Spécial. A complete description therefore needs the name, model year and, from 1961, the particular Rush engine.

Étoile: entry to the P60 shape

The Étoile joined the range after the initial P60 launch as an economy development of the Élysée. Club Simca France gives the Étoile 6 a 1,090 cc four-cylinder producing 42 hp. Its 6 CV fiscal rating and simpler finish lowered the entry price without depriving the buyer of the new body.

Thin stepped mouldings are a familiar sign of an early Étoile, but they are easily replaced. Extra chrome does not prove a higher model: dealers sold accessories and owners often embellished their cars. The block, registration papers, dashboard and fixing marks should support the base specification.

Élysée: the standard family saloon

The Élysée occupied the middle of the range. It is a four-door saloon with the 1,290 cc 7 CV engine, first in Flash form and then as a Rush for 1961. It combines family use with more equipment than an Étoile, without claiming the sporting character of the Montlhéry.

Its sales and long production life make it a common basis for restoration. They also made it a candidate for modification: a replacement engine, upholstery copied from another brochure, Montlhéry trim or Monaco accessories. An honestly restored Élysée retains all its practical appeal. A problem arises only when it is sold under a rarer name without persuasive records.

Montlhéry: the sporting model is still a saloon

The name of the banked circuit identifies the sporting branch. Montlhéry keeps four doors but has a more powerful mechanical specification and equipment suited to its status. In the first P60 period it belongs to the more highly tuned Flash-engine family. The range changed again after the introduction of the Rush.

In September 1961, Montlhéry Spéciale arrived with the 1,290 cc Rush Super M, advertised at 70 bhp. It should not be confused with every earlier Montlhéry. A painted rocker cover, replacement carburettor or “Spéciale” script does not prove that the complete power unit is present. Engine references, accessories and production date provide the necessary evidence.

Monaco: two doors and richer trim

Monaco is the coach in this selection. Door count and roof separate it immediately from the three saloons. Club Simca describes broad gold-coloured mouldings on early P60 Monacos, in contrast with the Étoile’s thin pieces. Two-tone paint, upholstery and brightwork supported its position, but the catalogues changed from year to year.

Monaco Spécial appeared alongside Montlhéry Spéciale with the 70 bhp Rush Super M. The club records metallic grey paint and a white Naugahyde interior for these two models. That documented combination is valuable evidence; it does not mean every Monaco left the factory that way, or that a car repainted in another colour is automatically wrong. The model year decides.

A short chronology prevents false comparisons

  • Autumn 1958, 1959 model year: launch of the P60 body with models including Élysée, Montlhéry and Monaco.
  • 1960 model year: the economy Étoile joins the range; Simca Talbot Club UK also notes a change to the saloon rear suspension.
  • October 1960, 1961 model year: introduction of the five-main-bearing Rush and changes to details including side trim and speedometer.
  • September 1961: Montlhéry Spéciale and Monaco Spécial launched with the Rush Super M.

The Club Simca register confirms that the names overlap. Listed Élysée P60s span 1958-1964, Montlhéry P60 precedes Montlhéry Spéciale, and Monaco precedes Monaco Spécial. These are club records of surviving vehicles rather than factory production totals. They help establish periods, but should not be quoted as the number made.

Inspect a car in the right order

  1. Body: four doors for Étoile, Élysée and Montlhéry; two for Monaco.
  2. Date: record manufacture and first registration without assuming that they are identical.
  3. Engine: separate 1,090 from 1,290 cc, Flash from Rush, and standard from Super derivatives.
  4. Interior: compare speedometer, fabrics, panels and controls with a brochure for the same year.
  5. Decoration: photograph mouldings, scripts and their fastenings before restoration.
  6. Records: retain registration papers, invoices, old photographs and references for removed parts.

A car can fail one point without losing its interest. An engine fitted in 1975 is part of its history. However, the price of a rare Monaco Spécial or Montlhéry Spéciale requires stronger proof than a converted saloon. Clear disclosure protects both buyer and vehicle.

The correct catalogue beats an accumulation of chrome

The many names served an effective sales strategy: one family could suit a limited budget, family duties, an interest in performance or the desire for an elegant coach. Today, that variety makes shortcuts dangerous. Door count, capacity, engine type and model year form the foundation; fabrics and ornaments then confirm the result or reveal a change.

The main Simca P60 page places the range in its period. For its engineering, see the guide to differences between Flash and Rush engines.
